name: Moddey Dhoo
aliases: the black dog of peel castle
description: The Moddey Dhoo, 'black dog' in Manx, is the phantom hound said to haunt Peel Castle on St Patrick's Isle. The legend rests chiefly on the account of the English topographer George Waldron, who recorded it in his Description of the Isle of Man (1731) under the phonetic form 'Mauthe Doog'. The dog was seen nightly in the castle rooms, above all in the guard chamber, and its appearances were long counted an omen of death.
appearance: A large black spaniel with curled, shaggy hair that was said to move silently through every room of the castle. It was big and shaggy enough to be likened to a calf or a great cocker: a coal-black hound that a single daring soldier once challenged as 'dog or devil'.
behavior: As soon as the candles were lit it came and lay down before the guard-room fire in the presence of all the soldiers, leaving at daybreak. The garrison grew so accustomed to it that they lost much of their terror, keeping quiet and respectful in its company. One night a drunken soldier boasted he would discover whether it was dog or devil and followed it into the corridor; horrible cries followed, and the man returned speechless and gibbering, dying three days later without ever telling what he had seen.
habitat: Peel Castle, St Patrick's Isle, Isle of Man
weaknesses: not seen since the soldier's death
cultural_significance: The Moddey Dhoo is the most famous ghost of the Isle of Man and a symbol of Peel Castle, promoted today by Manx National Heritage as the castle's best-known resident.
summary: The spectral black dog of Peel Castle, Isle of Man, first written down by George Waldron in 1731.
fun_fact: George Waldron is treated as the sole definitive written authority for the Peel Castle legend, which appeared in his Description of the Isle of Man in 1731 under the spelling 'Mauthe Doog'.
seo_title: Moddey Dhoo – Isle of Man Folklore
seo_description: The Moddey Dhoo: the spectral black dog of Peel Castle, Isle of Man.
source: George Waldron, Description of the Isle of Man (1731); A.W. Moore, Folk-Lore of the Isle of Man (1891); William Walter Gill; Manx National Heritage

name: Buggane
description: The Buggane is a huge, ogre-like, shapeshifting being of Manx folklore, sometimes likened to a Scandinavian troll. Its best-known feat was tearing the roof from St Trinian's Church at the foot of Greeba Mountain three times in a rage. Bugganes could not cross water or stand on hallowed ground, and were sometimes called upon by the fairies to punish mortals who had offended them.
appearance: Its natural form is described as covered with a mane of coarse black hair, with eyes like torches and glittering sharp tusks. It could also appear as a huge man with bull's horns and glowing eyes, as a great black calf, or as a human with the ears or hooves of a horse, and could grow large enough to wrench the roof off a church.
behavior: Malevolent and destructive, the Buggane tore the roof from St Trinian's Church whenever it was built, and could raise storms and wreck ships. One stowaway Buggane tried to wreck a ship bound for Ireland by driving it toward the rocky coast of Contrary Head until St Trinian's intervention turned the crew aside. A tailor named Timothy finally defied it, finishing a pair of breeches inside the church before fleeing as the monster hurled its head after him.
habitat: Slieu Whallian and Greeba Mountain, St Trinian's Church, Isle of Man; coastal caves near the sea
cultural_significance: The Buggane of St Trinian's remains one of the best-loved Manx tales, tied to the roofless chapel still visible near Greeba, and the creature gives its name to a beer brewed on the island.
summary: The malevolent shapeshifting giant of Manx folklore who tore the roof from St Trinian's Church.
fun_fact: In the legend, a Buggane once stowed away on a ship bound for Ireland and raised a storm to drive it back onto the rocks of Contrary Head, screaming 'St. Trinian should never have a whole church in Ellan Vannin'.
seo_description: The Buggane: the malevolent shapeshifting giant of Manx folklore who tore the roof off St Trinian's Church.
source: A.W. Moore, Folk-Lore of the Isle of Man (1891); Sophia Morrison, Manx Fairy Tales (1911); George Waldron (1731)

name: Glashtyn
description: The Glashtyn is a water-being of Manx folklore, recorded in Cregeen's Manx dictionary (1835) as a goblin or sprite and by Joseph Train (1845) as a water-horse that left its native element to mingle with land animals. It was sometimes given the hairy-goblin attributes of the fenodyree and sometimes the horse-like attributes of the cabbyl-ushtey, the Manx water horse, and in one reading was half-bovine and half-equine.
appearance: The Glashtyn could appear as a hairy goblin emerging from the water, or as a colt or sturdy grey or reddish-brown horse with uncanny eyes. In stories where it took human shape, its horse's ears were said to reveal its true nature.
behavior: It comes ashore to interact with humans and livestock and is dangerous to those who ride or trust it, luring them toward the water and dragging them to their death. The glen beneath Glen Meay Waterfall was said to be haunted by the ghost of a man who unwittingly rode the glashtyn and drowned at sea. In one tale it seized a woman by her dress before she escaped.
habitat: Lakes, rivers, coastal waters and waterfalls of the Isle of Man, especially Glen Meay Waterfall
cultural_significance: The Glashtyn is a central figure of Manx water-lore, bridging the brownie-like fairy and the Celtic water-horse, and appears across the collections of Train, Moore and Morrison.
summary: The shapeshifting water-spirit of Manx folklore, a hairy goblin in some tales and a dangerous water-horse in others.
fun_fact: A.W. Moore observed that the glashtin was 'sometimes ascribed the attributes of the fenodyree and sometimes those of the cabbyl-ushtey', the Manx water horse, and the glen beneath Glen Meay Waterfall was haunted by the ghost of a man who had ridden one to his drowning.
seo_description: The Glashtyn: the shapeshifting water-spirit of Manx folklore, hairy goblin and water-horse in one.
source: A.W. Moore, Folk-Lore of the Isle of Man (1891); Joseph Train, Historical and Statistical Account of the Isle of Man (1845); John Kelly, Fockleyr (1866); Cregeen's Dictionary (1835); Sophia Morrison

name: Tarroo Ushtey
description: The Tarroo Ushtey, or Manx water bull, is an amphibious creature of Manx folklore that lives in the sea or in lakes and comes ashore to mingle with ordinary cattle. George Waldron recorded the belief in the early 18th century that a cow that mated with it calved only a misshapen lump of flesh and skin without bones, often dying in the effort. It is a close cousin of the Scottish water-bull and distinct from the cabbyl-ushtey, the Manx water horse.
appearance: It has every semblance of a natural bull, though with a wild look and large eyes said to sparkle like fire. One Manx informant described it as half-cow and half-horse, a goblin shape linking it to the glashtyn.
behavior: It comes ashore at night to associate with and mate with domestic cattle, and it taunts people who try to catch it. Neighbours who cornered one stray in a herd and gave chase with pitchforks saw it dive into a river and escape, bobbing its head above the water as if mocking them.
habitat: Marshes, pools and coastal marshland, especially the northern lowlands around Andreas on the Isle of Man
cultural_significance: The Tarroo Ushtey appears in Waldron's early account and in later Manx folklore collections, where it is one of the island's distinct water-beings alongside the glashtyn and cabbyl-ushtey.
summary: The amphibious water-bull of Manx folklore that mates with domestic cattle and taunts its pursuers from the water.
fun_fact: George Waldron's early 18th-century account relates that a cow impregnated by the water-bull produces only 'a rude lump of flesh and skin without bones', and that neighbours once chased a suspected water-bull with pitchforks until it dived into a river and mocked them by bobbing its head.
seo_title: Tarroo Ushtey – Isle of Man Folklore
seo_description: The Tarroo Ushtey: the amphibious water-bull of Manx folklore that haunts the marshland of the Isle of Man.
source: George Waldron, Description of the Isle of Man (1731); A.W. Moore, Folk-Lore of the Isle of Man (1891); James MacKillop, A Dictionary of Celtic Mythology

name: Fenodyree
description: The Fenodyree is the Manx brownie, a hairy sprite of the fairy folk (ferrishyn) that helps humans with heavy farm work. One well-known story makes it a disgraced fairy who lost his place at the fairy court and was condemned to labour on the Isle of Man in a wild, hairy form. It threshes a whole barn of corn in a single night, moves great blocks of stone, and mows grass with stupendous speed.
appearance: Covered with copious body hair, the Fenodyree normally goes about naked, and is sometimes described as big and shaggy with fiery eyes, stronger than any man. Other accounts give it a height of only two feet, making it a giant among the Good People.
behavior: The creature works at night on behalf of farmers, driving home sheep and cutting or gathering hay before a storm. It takes grave offence if anyone offers it clothes, and a farmer of Ballochrink who left it a suit of garments saw it lift each one, recite the ailments it would bring, and depart to Glen Rushen with a melancholy wail. It once had so much trouble rounding up a hornless grey sheep that the 'sheep' turned out to be a hare.
habitat: Farms, glens and mountainsides of the Isle of Man, especially Glen Rushen, Glen Aldyn and the foot of Snaefell
weaknesses: driven off by gifts of clothing
cultural_significance: The Fenodyree is a signature figure of Manx folklore, the island's own brownie, and its story is preserved in the collections of Train, Moore and Morrison and echoed today in local art and place.
summary: The hairy Manx brownie who threshes barns and moves stones by night, and leaves forever if given clothes.
fun_fact: In the earliest written version the Phynnodderee was a fairy expelled from the fairy court for courting a Manx maid in Glen Aldyn during the harvest-moon (Re-hollys vooar yn ouyr); the Ballochrink farmer's gift of clothes made him recite, 'Cap for the head, alas poor head', and vanish into Glen Rushen.
seo_description: The Fenodyree: the hairy brownie of Manx folklore who labours for farmers and leaves when given clothing.
source: Joseph Train, Historical and Statistical Account of the Isle of Man (1845); A.W. Moore, Folk-Lore of the Isle of Man (1891); Sophia Morrison, Manx Fairy Tales (1911); Thomas Keightley, The Fairy Mythology

name: Mooinjer Veggey
description: The Mooinjer Veggey, Manx for 'little people', are the fairies of the Isle of Man, kin to the Aos Sí of the wider Gaelic world. They dwell in green hillsides and ancient tumuli, and their morality is famously ambiguous: they are neither good enough for Heaven nor bad enough for Hell, as Sophia Morrison put it. Belief in them was once as strong as belief in Christianity itself on the island.
appearance: Small creatures of two to three feet in height, otherwise very like mortals, who wear red caps and green jackets. They are most often seen on horseback followed by packs of little hounds of all the colours of the rainbow, and they are visible to people only when they choose to be.
behavior: They are inclined to be mischievous and spiteful, but some are benevolent, curing men of diseases and delivering them from misfortune. A musician lingering near their hills on a summer evening risked being entrapped by their delightful music. Islanders retired early on stormy nights so the weather-beaten fairies could enjoy the smouldering embers of the turf fire, left out bread and clean water, and refused to spin on Saturday evenings to keep their favour.
habitat: Green hillsides and ancient tumuli across the Isle of Man, especially Cronk Howe Mooar and the Fairy Bridge at Santon
weaknesses: warded off by iron and salt
cultural_significance: The Mooinjer Veggey are woven into everyday Manx life, from the greeting still expected of travellers crossing the Fairy Bridge to the running water, bread and fire customs once observed in every cottage, and their name now belongs to a Manx-language preschool charity.
summary: The Little People of Manx folklore, small red-capped green-jacketed fairies of the hills who are served bread and water and greeted at the Fairy Bridge.
fun_fact: Travellers crossing the Fairy Bridge on the New Castletown Road at Santon still call out 'Hello fairies!' or 'Moghrey mie mooinjer veggey!' (Good morning, little people), a greeting that islanders once considered necessary for safety.
seo_title: Mooinjer Veggey – Isle of Man Folklore
seo_description: The Mooinjer Veggey: the Little People of Manx folklore, the ambiguous fairies of the hills, bridges and tumuli.
source: A.W. Moore, Folk-Lore of the Isle of Man (1891); Sophia Morrison, Manx Fairy Tales (1911); Culture Vannin folklore records
